description: **ctx.out and the output member.** `ctx.out(text)` writes a command's answer to stdout, never hidden by `--quiet`; under `--json` the same bytes go into the document's new `output` member, and `interface_version` is now `3`. Consumers validating the document's key set must accept `output`.

**Prefixed warnings and errors.** In human mode `ctx.error` prints `error: <message>` and `ctx.warn` prints `warning: <message>` on stderr; `--json` diagnostics stay unprefixed. A handler that spelled its own `error: ` prefix now prints it twice.

**Early exit.** `strictcli.exit_now(code, message)` ends a command from anywhere in its call stack through the framework: `finally` blocks run, the message is printed as `error: <message>` or recorded in the `--json` diagnostics, and a dry run still renders its would-do log. `app.call()` raises `strictcli.ExitError` with the code and the message, and MCP answers `exit code <code>: <message>`.
**Payload renderers.** A command with a `payload_schema=` may declare `payload_renderer=`; human mode prints the rendering of the supplied payload, `--json` emits only the payload.
**Document writer.** `ctx.document()` gives an `owns_stdout=True` command a binary writer to the real stdout, unchanged in both modes.

**Runtime stdout guard under --json.** While a handler runs in machine mode, stdout is redirected: any byte written outside the framework (a `print`, `os.write(1, ...)`, an unmanaged child) fails the run with exit 1 and a diagnostic naming the bytes, and `os._exit` ends the run through the framework. Owns-stdout commands must write their document through `ctx.document()`.

**Child stdout under --json.** A child run through `ctx.effects.run(..., stream=True)` or `ctx.effects.spawn` no longer writes beside the `--json` document: its stdout is captured into the `output` member.

**Signals.** `app.run()` catches SIGINT and SIGTERM while the handler runs and sets `ctx.canceled`; when the handler returns, the command exits 130 or 143 with `error: canceled by signal <SIGNAL>`. A second signal gets the default action.

**--lint-framework-use.** Every app reserves `--lint-framework-use`, which scans the program's own package for process exits, direct stdout and stderr writes, argv access, and environment reads, and exits 1 listing each finding as `<path>:<line>: <rule>: <message>`.

A child started through `ctx.effects.spawn` that is still running when its handler ends is now killed (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after one second) and fails the run: exit 1 unless the status is already nonzero, plus `error: child process <pid> was still running when the handler ended and was killed: <argv>`. The exit step no longer waits for such a child. Wait on every child you spawn, or end it with the new `Spawned.kill()`; `Spawned.send_signal(signum)` sends any signal.
`ExitError` carries `payload`: what the command supplied through `ctx.payload` before its early exit, `None` when it supplied nothing.

The `config set`, `config init`, `config edit`, and `check` commands report their own errors as `error: <message>` and, under `--json`, as `error` diagnostics instead of bare stderr lines; a `check --tag` expression that does not parse is reported instead of crashing.

`check --ignore-warnings` and `run_checks(ignore_warnings=)` are removed: `check` stays the full report and exits nonzero on warnings, and the new `failing-checks` command (same selection flags) is the run where only error-level failures fail. Every `[checks.<name>]` in checks.toml must now declare `description` (one non-empty line) and `subject` (the options subject file its option belongs in: lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens, never `manifest`); a checks.toml lacking either is refused at construction with `checks.toml: check "<name>": missing required field "description"` (or `"subject"`), so add both to every declared check. `--dump-schema` publishes them on each check entry.

**Check values, `failing-checks`, and named hooks.** `app.set_check_value_resolver(fn)` lets an app assign each check `strictcli.CheckValue(value=..., source=...)`: `off` does not run the check (shown as an `OFF` row with its source), `warn` reports its failures as warnings, `error` runs it as registered; a value above the registered severity, outside the three, or without a source is refused. The new `failing-checks` command runs the same selection as `check` and prints only error-level failures, exiting nonzero exactly when one exists. `[hooks.<name>]` tables in checks.toml (`tag = "<expression>"`) name a selection that `check --hook <name>` and `failing-checks --hook <name>` run, and `check --list` shows each check's value and where it came from.

The check commands' `payload_schema` in `--dump-schema` lists `items` before `type`, as Go writes it, so a checks-enabled app's schema dump is byte-identical across the Python, Go, and TypeScript implementations.

Names follow one rule, refused where they are declared: command, group, deprecated-command, and long flag names (at every level, globals and choice scopes included), choice, constraint, tag, check, hook, grant, and update-resource names must be lowercase kebab-case of at least two characters (`[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*`), and a `short=` must be one ASCII letter (uppercase allowed). `help` and `version` are framework command names, refused for any command, group, or deprecated command at any depth. Rename a violating name, for example `@strictcli.flag("m", short="m", ...)` to `@strictcli.flag("message", short="m", ...)`; positional argument names and the App name are unaffected.
